rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Rescue of Minnie May Barry
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a red-haired girl in a heavy coat running with a lantern through deep snow toward a lamplit farmhouse window, fir trees white with snow, deep blue night, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Late one winter night Anne heard a frantic knocking at the Green Gables door. The night was bitter cold, and the snow lay deep on the lane. Diana stood outside, crying. “Minnie May has the croup,” she sobbed. “The grown-ups are all away, and nobody can go for the doctor. Oh, Anne, I am afraid she is dying.”
Anne runs through the falling snow to the Barry farmhouse.

Anne did not waste one minute. She pulled on her coat, and the two girls ran through the snow to the Barry farmhouse. Little Minnie May lay gasping in her cot. The hired girl could only wring her hands. But Anne had nursed croupy children before, in the homes where she had lived before Green Gables. Her voice shook, but her hands did not. “Keep hot water on the stove,” said Anne. “We must give her ipecac every minute till she is sick. Do exactly as I tell you, Diana.”
New word: croup — a winter illness that makes a child cough loudly and struggle to breathe. Warmth, calm courage, and a spoonful of ipecac every minute were Anne's weapons.

All night long the two girls fought for the little one. The kettle sang, and the snow flew past the windows, and Anne counted every minute between the spoonfuls. Toward morning the dreadful coughing began to ease. Minnie May fell asleep at last, breathing small and soft. When the doctor drove up at dawn, he looked at the child in wonder. “You have saved her life,” he told Anne. Diana, white and tired, smiled for the first time.

Mrs. Barry hurried home and took Anne's hands in both of her own. “I have been stubborn and blind,” she said. “You are the truest friend Diana ever had. Forgive me, child.” Anne forgave her before she finished speaking. From that day the two girls walked to school together again, and their friendship was deeper than before. The whole village heard by Sunday what Anne had done. That winter, Green Gables seemed a little brighter to Anne, because she had her bosom friend once more.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Miss Stacy Comes to Avonlea
chapters.artPrompt: a kind young teacher beside a chalkboard in a sunny country schoolroom, children raising hands at wooden desks, a red-haired girl beaming in the front row, morning light through tall windows, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Winter passed, and spring, and summer. When autumn came again, a new teacher arrived at the Avonlea school. Her name was Miss Stacy. She was young and bright, with kind eyes and a happy laugh. Miss Stacy had a way of listening with her chin in her hand. Even the naughtiest boys behaved for her, and the littlest ones watched her as if she were a storybook queen. Anne loved her by the second morning.
Miss Stacy smiles at her class in the bright Avonlea schoolroom.

School became the happiest place in the world. On Friday afternoons Miss Stacy let the pupils recite poems and act out little plays. One bright day she marched the whole school out to the woods to gather golden leaves and wild asters. Anne learned her lessons with her whole heart now, because Miss Stacy made everything seem worth knowing. “You can go far, Anne, if you keep on,” the teacher said once. Anne carried those words home like a small warm lamp.
New word: recite — to say a poem aloud from memory. Reciting before the whole school never frightened Anne for long.

Marilla said teachers came and went, and there was no use making a fuss over one more. But she watched Anne's shining face across the supper table, and said, dryly, that she was glad school pleased her. Diana sat beside Anne again, and the two friends shared their secrets on the walk home. Matthew said nothing at all. He only smiled into his teacup, for he had always known a girl was worth as much as a boy. And more.

Under Miss Stacy, Anne's marks climbed, and so did her dreams. She began to wonder about the world beyond Avonlea. Big schools, and colleges, and all the knowledge in all the books. She did not say these things aloud yet. But when she looked down the road toward White Sands, the sea glittered far off. Something in her heart leaned forward, waiting. The years ahead would ask much of her, and she was ready to give it.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Hat Full of Flowers
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl in a Sunday dress walking proudly toward a small white country church, her straw hat covered with pink wild roses and yellow buttercups, neighbours staring kindly, morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Everyone in Avonlea still laughed about Anne's very first Sunday at church, back in her first spring at Green Gables. Anne had never been to church in her life, and she wanted to look her best. A plain straw hat, she decided, was much too dull for such a grand day. So she picked wild roses by the lane, and buttercups from the field. She pinned them all over the brim until not a straw was left showing.
Anne arrives at church in her famous hat of roses and buttercups.

Anne walked down the aisle feeling like a queen in a garden. Nobody said a word, but Mrs. Rachel Lynde's eyes grew very round. After church Marilla saw the hat at last. At home she asked what on earth Anne had been thinking. “I thought it was exactly what fashionable ladies wear,” said Anne. Mrs. Lynde said she had never seen the like in her born days. On the walk home Diana giggled until she had to hold on to a fence. Anne could not understand what was funny.
Talk together: Anne loved to make plain things beautiful. How would you make a plain hat beautiful?

Marilla sighed the sigh of a woman who has explained things many times. Fashionable ladies, she said, did not wear whole gardens on their heads. Anne promised to wear her hat plain after that. But she did not promise to stop noticing flowers, and she never did. All her life, fields of buttercups would still stop her in the middle of the road. She would catch her breath and feel lucky.

In the end, the flowered hat did Anne more good than harm. The people of Avonlea decided that the new little girl was odd, and sweet, and honest, all at once. “That child has as many ideas as a calendar has days,” said Mrs. Lynde. “But there is no harm in her.” It was, in its way, the village's first welcome to Anne Shirley. And it made a very good story, told and retold for years.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · A Night at the Concert
chapters.artPrompt: a small red-haired girl reciting on a lamplit village hall stage before rows of neighbours in winter coats, her hands lifted mid-poem, warm lamplight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: That winter the people of Avonlea put on a concert in the village hall. The hall smelled of lamps and wet wool. The best scholars were to recite and sing, and Miss Stacy trained them every noon. Anne was to recite a poem all alone, on a real platform, before everybody she knew. She practiced in the barn, in the woodshed, and to the cows in the field. Even Josie Pye was to sing, which Anne said showed how fair Miss Stacy was.
Anne recites her poem on the little stage of the Avonlea hall.

The night of the concert, the hall was full from wall to wall. Anne waited behind the curtain with her heart drumming. Then her name was called, and she walked out, and the lamps blurred like stars. But when she began to speak, her voice rang out clear and sweet, and the hall went still. She made the people laugh, and then she made a grandmother wipe her eyes. When she stopped, the applause was like rain on a roof.
New word: platform — a raised floor you stand on so a whole crowd can see you. Anne stood on one at her very first concert.

Anne walked home through the snow with the Barrys, too happy to feel the cold. She told Diana every single moment of it twice. Diana squeezed her hand in the dark, and Anne squeezed back. The moon rode high over the white and silent fields. At Green Gables she lit a candle and told it all again to Marilla. Marilla said concerts were foolishness, but asked, all the same, whether the hall had been full.

Matthew had waited up too. He said only, “I heard it went well.” But his face shone. Josie Pye sang her song nicely, and everyone clapped politely. For days afterward, when he met the neighbours at the store, they praised his girl to him. Each time, he drove home sitting a little straighter. Anne decided that being praised was sweet, but being proud of someone you love is sweeter. Upstairs, in the cold little east gable, she fell asleep still bowing.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Walk on the Ridgepole
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl in a pinafore walking with outstretched arms along the narrow peak of a wooden shed roof, schoolgirls gasping below in a green yard, bright afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: When spring came, the schoolgirls fell into the habit of daring each other. They walked fence rails to prove their courage, then beams, then higher things. The boys dared each other too, but somehow the girls' dares were the fiercest. Josie Pye, who had a sharp tongue, said one noon that Anne Shirley was afraid to try anything really hard. Every girl in the schoolyard turned to look.
Anne walks the ridgepole while the schoolgirls hold their breath.

Anne went pale, and then determined. She would show Josie Pye. Not far away stood a long woodshed, with a narrow ridgepole running along its roof. Diana begged her not to try. Anne climbed up, stood straight, and began to walk. For three steps she was magnificent. Then her heel slipped on the smooth wood. She wavered, threw out her arms, and fell heavily to the ground.
New word: sprain — to twist a joint so that it swells and hurts. Anne's ankle was badly sprained, and she lay on the sofa for weeks.

The other girls screamed and crowded around. Anne could not stand; her ankle was swelling fast. It was Gilbert Blythe who came running. He lifted Anne as if she weighed nothing. “Don't be afraid,” he said quietly. “I have you.” He set her gently in his buggy and drove her home without one word of teasing. The lane had never seemed so long. Marilla went white when she saw Anne's face. Anne lay against the seat, too sore to look at anybody.

The doctor came and strapped the ankle. Even Marilla praised Gilbert's driving. For weeks Anne read books on the sofa while the girls came to visit. “You might thank Gilbert properly,” said Diana. “It was very handsome of him.” “I know it,” said Anne slowly. “I said the words, but I did not say them kindly, and that is the truth.” Being rescued by Gilbert, of all people, stung her pride worse than the ankle. Somewhere inside her, something old and stubborn sat down again.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Haunted Wood
chapters.artPrompt: a frightened red-haired girl running with a basket down a dark spruce-wood path at dusk, pale mist between black tree trunks, one white shape glowing ahead, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Between Green Gables and the Barry farm lay a thick spruce wood. It was so dark at noon that it felt like evening. For fun, one summer, the girls gave it a name: the Haunted Wood. They peopled it with ghosts — a white lady, a weeping child, and worse things besides. All that summer the ghosts grew more real. At last the girls would not go near the wood after sundown at all.
Anne runs through the dark spruce wood with her basket.

It was exciting — until they believed it. Diana half believed, and Anne believed entirely, because she had invented it. Then one evening Marilla sent Anne through the wood on an errand to Diana's house. Marilla had no patience with nonsense. It was just as the light was dying. Anne begged. “It is only spruce trees,” said Marilla. “Ghosts do not run errands, but girls do.” And she handed Anne the basket.
Talk together: Anne scared herself with her own stories. Have you ever done that? What helped you feel brave again?

The wood was grey and silent, and every stump wore a shadow like a hood. Anne walked as fast as her shaking legs allowed. Then, beside the path, something white fluttered. That was too much. With a shriek, Anne flew the rest of the way. She burst in at the Barrys' door white as milk, with her heart hammering. It took a glass of milk and Diana's arm around her before she could speak.

She never learned what the white shape was — probably a bush moving in the wind. She never needed to know. That night Anne gave up the Haunted Wood forever. Marilla, listening at the stairs, laughed until she had to sit down. The basket was never recovered, and nobody asked about it. After that, Anne kept her imagination for better things: for stories, for sunsets, and for friends. A mind that can invent a ghost can invent almost anything. So it must be handled with care.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Minister's Wife
chapters.artPrompt: a sweet young minister's wife in a lavender dress greeting a red-haired girl at a flower-covered gate, a white parsonage behind them, warm summer light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Early in the summer, Avonlea got a new young minister, Mr. Allan, and his wife. Mrs. Allan was still almost a girl herself, with soft eyes and a smile that made people tell her things. The whole village agreed the Allans were a gift, and every garden sent flowers to the manse that first week. Anne loved Mrs. Allan within five minutes, and loved her more every Sunday after. Even Mrs. Rachel Lynde approved, and she did not approve of everybody.
Anne meets kind Mrs. Allan at the manse gate.

Anne decided that Mrs. Allan was the most beautiful person, inside and out, she had ever known. She began, secretly, to try to be better. Anne meant to prove herself worthy. “If I could only be good the way Mrs. Allan is good,” Anne told Marilla. Marilla said goodness was mostly washing dishes and doing your duty. But even she was gentler that month.
New word: manse — the house where a minister and the minister's family live.

Then came the proudest news: Mr. and Mrs. Allan were coming to tea at Green Gables on Friday. Marilla planned the meal like a battle. Marilla even let Anne use the best tablecloth. Anne begged to make the cake — a real layer cake, all by herself. Marilla, against her own habit, said yes. After all, a girl could not learn without trying. Anne floated on air for two whole days.

Anne rose early on Friday and baked in a dream of glory. The kitchen smelled like happiness. She washed the good milk dishes twice over. The cake came out of the oven golden and high. It was, Anne told the window, the most beautiful thing she had ever made. She set it on the best dish, where nobody could miss it. Only one thing worried her: it must be perfect. Mrs. Allan deserved perfect. Anne waited for evening the way children wait for Christmas morning.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Cake with Painkiller in It
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl holding a golden two-layer cake in a farmhouse kitchen while a grey-haired woman discovers a small medicine bottle on the shelf, late afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The great evening came. The lamp was trimmed, the fire leapt in the stove, and Anne's heart leapt with it. The Allans sat in the parlour, and Mrs. Allan praised the flowers and the clean tablecloth. When tea was served, Anne brought in her layer cake, blushing like a peony. Mrs. Allan took a large piece, and so did Marilla. Anne watched them, happiness stacked as high as her frosting.
Anne serves her beautiful cake to Mrs. Allan.

Then Mrs. Allan's fork stopped. Marilla tasted her own piece and frowned. “Anne, what did you flavour this cake with?” “Vanilla,” said Anne proudly — and then, catching Marilla's eye, not so proudly. Marilla marched to the pantry and came back holding a small bottle. “Anne Shirley, you have flavoured your cake with my anodyne liniment. I keep it on the second shelf, and you took the wrong bottle.” The kitchen was very quiet.
New word: liniment — a strong-smelling medicine rubbed on sore shoulders, never poured into cake batter.

Anne flew to her room and flung herself on the bed. To give the minister's wife painkiller cake — she could not have felt worse on purpose! In a few minutes there was a soft knock. Mrs. Allan sat down on the edge of the bed. She did not scold. She laughed a little, kindly. Everyone spoils things sometimes, she said. The very best cooks have all baked one terrible cake. “You will bake a hundred good ones,” she told Anne. “And you will laugh at this one first.”
Talk together: Anne made a big mistake and was forgiven kindly. What helps you feel better after a mistake?

Anne came down to supper after all, eyes still pink. Marilla said the less said about cakes the better, and forbade herself a smile, not very successfully. And that was not quite the end. Before she left, Mrs. Allan invited Anne to come to tea at the manse, just the two of them. The worst evening of the summer turned into the promise of the best one. Anne learned that a mistake, kindly handled, can end sweeter than a perfect cake.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · Tea at the Manse
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl taking tea with a kind young woman in a bright parlour, thin china cups and roses on the table, slanting golden afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: On the appointed afternoon, Anne put on her second-best dress and walked to the manse with her heart beating happily. She had brushed her hair until it shone like copper — “the one thing it can do,” Anne said. Mrs. Allan met her at the door as if she had been waiting for her all day. The parlour was full of afternoon light. Flowers from Avonlea gardens stood on the table, and the teacups were thin as flower petals. Anne was careful as a cat.
Anne pours out her heart to Mrs. Allan over tea.

It was, Anne said afterward, the most beautiful afternoon of her whole life. Mrs. Allan poured tea with her own hands. They talked about books, and Avonlea, and the poplar shadows on the parlour floor. Then, somehow, Anne found herself telling her everything. Every scrape she had ever fallen into — the apology, the wine, the hat of buttercups. Mrs. Allan did not laugh at her. She laughed with her, and Anne's heart felt washed clean.
New word: scrapes — small troubles you get yourself into. Anne collected scrapes the way other girls collect ribbons.

“You will laugh at all this someday,” said Mrs. Allan, “and so shall I. But neither of us will be done living.” Anne walked home under a sky striped with pearl and rose. She felt brave and new. It came to her that being good was not a cage, the way she had once feared. It was more like a garden — and Mrs. Allan had left the gate open.

She told Marilla every bite of the meal and every word of the talk, twice. Marilla listened longer than usual. “That woman,” she said at last, “has a way with girls.” It was the highest praise Marilla knew. That night Anne made a quiet decision. She could not be good all at once. But she could be good a little at a time, the way Mrs. Allan would want. Anne's happiness that week was quiet and deep, like a well.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · The Lily Maid of Astolat
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl lying solemnly in a wooden boat on a pond at sunset, a black shawl over her body and a white lily in her folded hands, girls watching from the shore, storybook illustration

blocks.text: That summer the girls found a poem they loved more than any other. It was the story of Elaine, the Lily Maid of Astolat. She died for love, and was carried down the river in a barge, with a lily in her hand. Anne knew exactly how it should be done. The Barry pond would be the river. The old flat — a flat wooden boat — would be the barge. And she, of course, would be Elaine.
Anne lies in the flat as the Lily Maid of Astolat.

On a still, golden evening they laid Anne in the flat, straight and pale. Her hair was unbound, a black shawl was folded over her, and a pond lily lay in her folded hands. The plan was simple. The flat would drift down the pond and land near the old bridge. There the other girls would be waiting to receive the Lily Maid. Diana and Jane pushed the barge off from the shore. Elaine floated away, trying her best to look dead.
New word: flat — a flat-bottomed boat used for crossing farm ponds. This one should have retired years before.

But plans on water go as water pleases. Halfway down the pond, Anne felt cold water about her ankles. The old flat was leaking badly, and beginning to settle. Anne sat up in a hurry, funeral dignity and all. She reached the bridge pile and clung to it, with the shawl streaming and the lily floating away. The barge of the Lily Maid of Astolat sank quietly beneath her.

The girls on shore were screaming. It was Gilbert, rowing past in his boat, who reached her first. He pulled alongside and lifted her in, dripping. What on earth, he asked, was the Lily Maid of Astolat doing clinging to a bridge pile? Anne, mortified beyond words, told him. He rowed her to the landing without laughing — almost without laughing. “Thank you,” said Anne at the landing, in her politest and coldest voice.

Gilbert lifted his cap and rowed away across the shining water. Anne walked home with wet shoes and a burning face. All evening she wished she had said something warmer. For one moment she had wanted to be gracious — and pride had spoken instead. It would be a long time before the chance came again.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · Puffed Sleeves
chapters.artPrompt: a shy elderly man watching a red-haired girl unwrap a soft brown dress with big puffed sleeves on Christmas morning, firelight and a small tree, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Matthew had one private sorrow that winter. Sitting at church, Matthew had noticed something. Every girl in Avonlea wore dresses with big puffed sleeves — every girl but Anne. Anne's sleeves were plain and tight, for Marilla cut all her dresses for use, not for beauty. “They have sleeves like balloons,” thought Matthew, “and my girl has sleeves like strings.” It seemed to him, without his being able to say it, that this was not quite fair.
Anne unwraps the Christmas dress with its beautiful puffed sleeves.

Matthew did what he could. He rode into Carmody one day, meaning to buy a dress himself. It was the boldest thing he had done in years. But the store was full, the clerks were busy, and Matthew could not make his mouth say “puffed sleeves.” After an hour of misery he slipped out and drove home with an empty buggy and a red face. A bashful man does not shop for dresses.
Talk together: Matthew showed his love with deeds, not words. How do the people around you show love to you?

Then he did a clever thing, for a shy man: he went to Mrs. Rachel Lynde. She understood in one minute and promised to manage everything. And on Christmas morning there was a parcel on Anne's chair. Inside was a soft brown dress, and the sleeves were puffed. Puffed as grandly as any sleeve in Charlottetown.

Anne held the dress up and could not speak. “Oh, Matthew,” she whispered at last, “you remembered.” Matthew went red to the ears and said it was nothing. Marilla confessed she had frowned at the sleeves all through the making. But when Anne put it on, she felt like a new girl in a new world. Anne's joy could be heard from the road. The sleeves, she said, made her feel she ought to be very, very good. That night she hung the dress over a chair where she could see it first thing in the morning.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · The Story Club
chapters.artPrompt: four girls in winter dresses reading papers aloud around a lamplit farm table, one red-haired girl standing and gesturing dramatically, cosy firelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: That winter Anne founded the Story Club. The members were herself, Diana, Jane Andrews, and Ruby Gillis. They met every week, in turn, in one another's houses. The rules were strict: each member had to read aloud one story of her own making. Anne wrote the rules herself, on the first page of a scribbler. She was elected president by a vote of four to none. Diana was made secretary, and wrote the minutes in violet ink.
Anne reads her latest dramatic story to the Story Club.

Anne's stories were the longest and the most terrible. Her heroines were beautiful and tragic. Most of them died magnificently of broken hearts, or nearly died, until Anne grew kinder to them. The club voted her stories the best, mostly because they were the longest. Diana wrote love stories, Jane wrote sensible ones, and Ruby's were full of lords and ladies. The biscuits were voted into the rules at the second meeting. Everyone agreed biscuits helped the plots.
New word: plot — the chain of happenings in a story. A good plot, the club agreed, must never stand still.

Marilla said the club was all very well if the dishes were done. Mrs. Lynde worried that so much imagination was unhealthy. Matthew quietly asked for one of Anne's stories to be read to him twice. Anne read him the one about the haunted ship, twice. Anne said people who never made up stories were missing half the world. Diana agreed with everyone. In Green Gables, a person could believe whichever of these she liked.

The club lasted all winter, and it taught Anne more than she expected. She learned that a story must be built, not just dreamed. She learned that people in books must act like real people. She learned that even tragedy is better with a little laughter in it. All her life she would remember those winter afternoons. The fire, the rustling paper, and four girls learning to make believe on purpose.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · Green Hair
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl staring in horror at her green-dyed hair in a kitchen mirror while a grey-haired woman holds scissors, morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Anne had one great sorrow in life, and it never left her: her red hair. She had been teased about it, and no teasing stung worse. So when a peddler came to the door one afternoon with a bottle, Anne listened. He swore the liquid would dye her hair a beautiful, glossy black. The bottle cost a whole summer's egg money. Anne paid it before her conscience could say a word.
Anne discovers what the peddler's dye has done.

She hid the bottle under her bed until the house was asleep. She dyed her hair that very night. All through her dreams she saw herself with raven-black braids. In the morning she crept to the glass, half in fear and half in hope — and screamed. Her hair was green. Not slightly green, but green as spring grass, green as bottle glass. Every strand of it.
New word: dye — a liquid that changes the colour of hair or cloth. Cheap dye keeps its promises rarely.

Marilla was horrified, and then, in secret, helpless with laughter. There was nothing to do but cut. Marilla took the scissors. The green curls fell on the kitchen floor until what was left was short as a boy's. Diana held the comb. “It serves me right,” said Anne, who was honest even in disaster. “I was vain, and I tried to change what cannot be changed. I shall never believe a peddler again.” And she never did.

At school the next Monday the girls stared, and Josie Pye giggled. Anne held her head high, which was easier without all that hair to carry. Diana said short hair suited Anne, which was not true, but was friendship. Marilla kept a straight face, barely. Her hair grew in as red as ever, and she was through with dye forever. Even Anne had to laugh at last. If her hair must be famous for being red, it would be famous, at least, for being clean and bright.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · A Great Ambition
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl sitting by a lit farmhouse window at dusk with a stack of books and a lamp, dreaming, warm lamplight against a blue evening, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One spring evening, when Anne was nearly fifteen, Miss Stacy asked her best pupils to stay after school. The classroom was very quiet. There was, she told them, a place called Queen's Academy in Charlottetown. There girls and boys were trained to be teachers. In two years there would be an entrance examination. Anyone who wished to work for it could join a special class. Anne's heart stood still, and then began to beat very fast.
Anne dreams of Queen's Academy over her books.

She walked home holding the dream like a full cup. Marilla said she had never seen the use of so much learning for a girl. Grammar, she said, had never yet baked a loaf. But Matthew, at the stove, said quietly that no child of theirs should be held back for want of schooling. Anne promised to earn her keep with extra chores, and did. Marilla looked at Matthew, and then at Anne's burning eyes, and said it would be as they wished.
New word: academy — a school for higher learning. Queen's Academy trained teachers for the schools of Prince Edward Island.

Anne could hardly sleep for joy. To study, really study, with Miss Stacy's blessing — and to teach, someday, in a schoolhouse of her own! “I want to know everything,” she told Diana on the way home from school. “If I cannot have everything, I shall take a great deal.” Diana laughed, and said she would take the world a little more slowly herself. The maples were in leaf, and everything seemed possible.

There was hard work ahead, and Anne knew it. But she had learned by now that wishing is only the first step, and walking is all the rest. Green Gables settled into a new rhythm. There were chores, lessons, supper, and the lamp in the east gable burning later and later. Even the hens seemed to approve. Marilla never said so, but she was proud of that light.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · The Queen's Class
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl and a brown-haired boy seated at opposite school desks piled with books, both writing fast, autumn light through tall school windows, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The special class began that autumn. Anne, Gilbert Blythe, and several more Avonlea scholars studied after hours for Queen's. There were long lists to learn and long evenings to learn them in. Miss Stacy met them on Fridays. She gave hard questions and warm praise, and occasionally frightened them with practice examinations. The Avonlea school buzzed like a hive all winter with the doings of the Queen's class. Diana listened outside the window and took notes of her own.
Anne and Gilbert study neck and neck for Queen's.

From the first week it was a race between two: Anne Shirley and Gilbert Blythe. If Anne led one week, Gilbert led the next. He seemed to learn easily, almost lazily, which maddened her. “He remembers everything,” she complained to her candle. “It is very annoying in a boy.” She studied as if studying were a weapon. The candle did not complain. It burned down as a witness.
Talk together: Anne and Gilbert each worked harder because of the other. Has a friendly rival ever helped you do your best?

Yet it was not really hate, though Anne called it so. You do not count someone's marks so carefully unless you count on them, too. Sometimes, when Gilbert said something clever in class, Anne caught herself almost smiling. Then she stopped herself in time, as she believed honour demanded. The slate, after all, had never been forgiven. Still, it was a comfortable sort of anger, like a warm coat.

Diana was not in the class. Still, she waited for Anne every day at the lane, and heard every triumph and groan twice. The winter passed in ink and recitation. Spring came, and the class grew smaller as some decided an entrance examination was more than they had bargained for. Anne never once thought of quitting. Miss Stacy said the class was the pride of her heart. Anne's motto that winter was simple: no surrender. The harder it grew, the higher Anne lifted her chin.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 · Two Roads for Two Friends
chapters.artPrompt: two girls leaning on a pasture gate at sunset, one red-haired and one dark-haired, a still lake shining behind them, golden evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One golden evening in autumn, Anne and Diana walked home the long way, past the Lake of Shining Waters. The water lay like a mirror, and a heron stood in the shallows, thinking heron thoughts. A kingfisher flashed across the water like a blue spark. They had walked this way a hundred times, but this time they walked slowly. They had something to talk about that neither of them liked. Anne was deep in the Queen's class. Diana was not in it, and would not be. Her road lay at home.
Anne and Diana talk by the gate as the sun goes down.

“It is not that I could not,” said Diana. “It is that I do not want to, not really. And Mother needs me. Sometimes I feel dull beside you, Anne, with your Latin and your lists.” Anne stopped right there in the lane. “You are the truest heart I know,” she said. “Books are only one room in the house of the world, and you have the whole house already.”
Talk together: You and your best friend may love different things. What do you share that never changes?

They stood a while at the lane gate and talked until the light went amber. Diana would learn all the arts of home, and Anne would learn every lesson ever set. Their roads would run side by side, even when they ran apart. That, they promised, holding hands on the bars of the gate, was a vow. They shook hands on it, solemnly, the way heroines do. Anne said Diana's name in her heart whenever she needed courage, and it always worked.

It was the kind of promise grown people smile at. But for the two of them it came true. The years would take Anne far and keep Diana near. But walking home that evening, under the first star, neither girl doubted they would be friends forever. Some friendships are for seasons; theirs, both girls were sure, was for life.
